issues.legal_issue: A lease covenant requiring a tenant to keep premises in the condition received obliges the tenant to make repairs needed to maintain them, and negligent breach causing damage can support eviction under the rent-control law.
material_facts: The lease required the tenant to keep the premises in as good a condition as when received, except for reasonable wear and tear and specified causes of damage.
The lower courts found that the premises had deteriorated because of the tenant’s negligence in upkeep and maintenance, rather than reasonable wear and tear.
The lease placed the repair obligation on the tenant, contrary to the rent-control law’s default allocation of repair responsibility to the landlord.
issues.conclusion: The covenant required the tenant to maintain the premises in good condition and tenantable repair. The tenant’s negligent failure to do so breached the lease term and entitled the landlord to possession under the rent-control law.
issues.legal_principle: The wording requiring a tenant to keep premises in the same good condition and deliver them up in that condition imposes an ongoing duty to make necessary repairs and prevent permissive waste. The Court relied on Luxmore v. Robson, Lurcott v. Wakely & Wheeler, and Doongersey v. Keshavji Meghji. Under Section 23(1) of the Bombay Rent Act, 1947, the landlord bears the duty to keep premises in good and tenantable repair only in the absence of an agreement to the contrary. A tenant’s breach of an essential lease term can entitle the landlord to possession under the latter part of Section 12(1) of that Act.

predicates.eviction_claim_under_rent_control: The landlord sought eviction in a proceeding governed by a rent-control regime.
predicates.lease_requires_tenant_to_maintain_premis: The lease required the tenant to keep the premises in the condition in which they were received and to return them in that condition.
predicates.tenant_negligently_failed_to_maintain_pr: The tenant negligently failed to maintain or repair the premises as required by the lease.
predicates.damage_exceeded_reasonable_wear_and_tear: The deterioration or damage resulted from the tenant’s failure to maintain the premises and was not attributable to reasonable wear and tear or an excepted cause.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim under rent control rests on a lease requiring the tenant to maintain the premises, and negligent failure causes damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, the landlord is entitled to possession for the tenant’s breach.

issues.legal_issue: Rent-control protection is unavailable for appropriated cantonment accommodation when the eviction suit predates the extension of the rent-control law and the extension does not apply to pending suits; after valid termination, possession may be sought under the general law.
material_facts: The premises were situated in a cantonment and had been appropriated by the Central Government under legislation concerning house accommodation in cantonments.
The eviction suit was filed before the Bombay Rent Act was extended to the cantonment.
The later extension excluded the provision that would have applied the Act to pending suits, and appropriated accommodation was exempt under the extension legislation.
The tenancy had been terminated by a proper notice to quit, and that fact was pleaded and not disputed.
issues.conclusion: The tenant did not have the protection of the Bombay Rent Act. The landlord was entitled under the Transfer of Property Act to seek eviction on termination of the tenancy, even though the lease did not reserve a right of re-entry for breach of its repair covenant.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 3 of the Cantonments (Extension of Rent Control Laws) Act, 1957, the relevant extension did not apply the Bombay Rent Act, 1947 to pending suits because Section 50 of that Act was excluded from the extension. In addition, clause (c) of the proviso to Section 3 exempted appropriated accommodation from the extended rent-control law. Without that protection, the landlord could seek eviction under the Transfer of Property Act on termination of the tenancy; the absence of a contractual right of re-entry affected eviction for breach of the lease term, not eviction following termination of the tenancy.

rule.if: eviction_suit and premises_are_appropriated_cantonment_accommodation and suit_predates_rent_control_extension and extension_does_not_cover_pending_suits and tenancy_was_validly_terminated

predicates.eviction_suit: The proceeding is a suit by a landlord seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.premises_are_appropriated_cantonment_acc: The premises are in a cantonment and have been appropriated by the government as accommodation under a law governing cantonment housing.
predicates.suit_predates_rent_control_extension: The eviction suit was filed before the rent-control law was extended to the relevant cantonment.
predicates.extension_does_not_cover_pending_suits: The extension of the rent-control law does not make it applicable to suits already pending when the extension takes effect.
predicates.tenancy_was_validly_terminated: The landlord gave a proper notice to quit that terminated the tenancy.

issues.definition: For an eviction suit concerning appropriated cantonment accommodation, if the suit predates an extension that does not cover pending suits and the tenancy was validly terminated, the tenant lacks rent-control protection and the landlord may seek possession under general law.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may consider a new legal ground that depends only on admitted facts and requires no investigation or proof of additional facts.
material_facts: The landlord raised in the Supreme Court the contention that the rent-control law did not apply to the premises.
The contention depended on the premises’ location and appropriation and on the legal effect of the extension of the rent-control law, matters the Court treated as undisputed or admitted.
The landlord had pleaded that the tenancy was terminated by notice, and the tenant had not put that fact in issue.
issues.conclusion: The Court permitted consideration of the new contention because it was a question of law that required no investigation into or proof of new facts.
issues.legal_principle: A pure question of law may be raised at the appellate stage when its determination does not require investigation into or proof of new facts. The Court applied this principle to the admitted facts before it and cited no earlier case for this point.

rule.if: appellate_challenge_to_eviction and new_ground_is_a_question_of_law and material_facts_are_admitted and deciding_ground_requires_no_new_fact_finding

predicates.appellate_challenge_to_eviction: The proceeding is an appellate challenge to a decision in an eviction dispute.
predicates.new_ground_is_a_question_of_law: A party raises a legal ground that was not relied on in the courts below.
predicates.material_facts_are_admitted: The facts necessary to decide the new ground are admitted or undisputed.
predicates.deciding_ground_requires_no_new_fact_fin: The court can decide the ground without investigating or proving any additional facts.

issues.definition: In an appellate eviction challenge, a new legal ground may be considered when the necessary facts are admitted and deciding the ground requires no new fact-finding.
